name: snap (Rust Snappy, BurntSushi/rust-snappy)
workload: Snappy raw-format compress and decompress of the 12 files of the C++ library's own microbenchmark corpus (html, urls, jpg, pdf, txt1-4, pb, gaviota), both libraries driven by the same harness.
claimed_speedup: README: performance 'should roughly match' C++ Snappy on x86_64. From the README ratio columns (C++ column over snap column): decompress uflat07_txt2 916.6 vs 1001.8 MB/s (snap 1.09x faster), uflat09_txt4 857.2 vs 930.2 MB/s (1.09x), uflat03_jpg_200 1.08x, uflat06_txt1 1.08x, uflat08_txt3 1.07x, uflat01_urls 1.04x; compress zflat03_jpg_200 1.10x faster, zflat11_gaviota 1.07x faster. Losses: decompress uflat04_pdf C++ 1.10x faster, uflat10_pb 1.05x, compress zflat01_urls 1.04x, zflat10_pb 1.02x.
compiler_and_flags: Not stated for either side (README only says both used the same benchmark harness).
tradeoffs: Compression output is byte-for-byte identical to the C++ library (README); also provides the Snappy frame format; pure Rust with no C++ dependency, so no FFI or build-time C++ toolchain.
caveats: This is a parity result, not a clear win: the Rust crate is faster on about half the rows (by up to 10%) and slower on others (by up to 10%), and the README itself only claims it should 'roughly match' C++. Numbers are from an old setup (Snappy/C++ 1.1.8, i7-6900K) and the build flags of both sides are not stated, so tier A is not met. First-party measurement by the crate author. A newer Snappy 1.2.x was not tested.
found_via: GitHub: raw README of BurntSushi/rust-snappy, opened while sweeping well-known Rust ports of C/C++ libraries for in-repo C++ comparison tables; the repo is not in KNOWN_LIST (google/snappy is).

name: ckmeans (Rust optimal 1-D k-means) vs Ckmeans.1d.dp C++
baseline: Ckmeans.1d.dp C++ implementation (kmeans_1d_dp, methods 'linear' (default) and 'loglinear'; the code behind the R package and the ckmeans-1d-dp Python package), vendored in bench_cpp
workload: Optimal 1-D k-means (dynamic programming) on seeded random inputs: Uniform(1,3) and Uniform(0,1000) at n = 110,000 and 1,000,000, k from 3 to 50, a bimodal normal input, and BIC selection of k in 1..9; Criterion point estimates, one run of the full suite.
claimed_speedup: bench_cpp/README.md (Criterion, ms): Uniform(1,3) n=110,000 k=5 rust_indices 13.2 vs cpp_linear 26.0 and cpp_loglinear 25.3; k=20 49.7 vs 105.3 / 90.7; n=1,000,000 k=5 126.7 vs 254.9 / 249.8; k=20 513.5 vs 995.4 / 940.5; Uniform(0,1000) n=110,000 k=3 7.6 vs 16.5 / 16.1, k=50 114.4 vs 256.0 / 193.0; BIC selection n=110,000 rust_optimal 26.7 vs 54.5 / 50.9, n=1,000,000 263.1 vs 510.2 / 515.9. About 1.6x to 2.3x faster than C++ in every row, counting the slowest Rust variant (rust_optimal, which includes the BIC step) against the faster C++ method (derived from page data); the repository's PR #41 summary says 'Rust is 23 to 48 % faster than the C++ code in all cases'.
compiler_and_flags: rustc 1.99.0 with the bench_cpp release profile lto = true, codegen-units = 1 (same as the ckmeans_py release build); C++ sources compiled by build.rs with -O3 -DNDEBUG -std=c++11 using Apple clang 17.0.0 (no LTO, no -march stated).
tradeoffs: The vendored C++ code is LGPL-3.0-or-later and the Rust crate is BlueOak-1.0.0. Rust ckmeans_indices returns sorted data plus index ranges rather than per-value labels; the C++ call also returns labels, centres and sizes, and the Rust wrapper needs a mutex because kmeans_1d_dp() sorts through a static pointer. Results are identical to the scalar search (README).
caveats: Library win, not a language-level claim. Different implementations of the same objective: the Rust crate uses a flat matrix, a stack-based divide-and-conquer column fill with a single-pass inner loop and a vectorised split-point search (fearless_simd), while the C++ code is scalar; so the speedup mixes engineering, algorithm constant factors and SIMD. The C++ default call also does a BIC step (6 to 10 percent of its time) that rust_indices and rust_clusters skip; rust_optimal does it and is still faster. Single run of the suite on one aarch64 laptop, benchmark written by the crate author; the bench_cpp crate and its results were added in October 2026 commits (PR description links a Claude Code session). BlueOak-1.0.0 is a permissive licence that is not on the OSI-approved list, so usability is set to reference per the rubric; the orchestrator may override.
found_via: WebSearch: 'Rust crate README benchmark comparison with C++ library faster than abseil OR folly OR boost ...' surfaced urschrei/ckmeans PR #41; then opened bench_cpp/README.md, the crate README, Cargo.toml files and the commits page.
why_faster: Source (README, 'Implementation' table): flat contiguous matrix for cache locality, stack-based divide-and-conquer column fill with a single-pass inner loop that computes the sum of squares once per candidate (the two-pointer approach computes it twice), pre-allocated stack, and a vectorised split-point search with run-time SIMD selection.

name: simdjzon (Zig port of simdjson)
baseline: simdjson (C++) DOM parser built from the amalgamated simdjson.cpp
workload: Whole-process run that parses and validates twitter.json (the simdjson sample file) once, measured with the 'poop' tool over about 2,000 runs per binary.
claimed_speedup: README 'benchmark vs simdjson - 5/7/26': wall_time 2.39 ms (simdjson) vs 2.08 ms (simdjzon), 12.9% lower; peak_rss 5.22 MB vs 2.35 MB (55% lower); cpu_cycles 2.39M vs 1.97M (17.5% lower); cache_misses 24.1K vs 5.52K (77% lower); branch_misses 21.5K vs 7.02K (67% lower); instructions 5.28M vs 5.37M (1.7% higher).
compiler_and_flags: simdjson: g++ (GCC) 15.2.1 20260123, g++ main.cpp simdjson.cpp -o simdjson -O3 -march=native. simdjzon: Zig master with -Drelease-fast (README usage; exact Zig version and target CPU flags not stated).
tradeoffs: README warns 'work in progress, expect bugs and/or missing features'; ondemand get_string has bugs in release-small builds; needs AVX (x86_64) and prefers CLMUL, no fallback for CPUs without them; PowerPC unsupported; tracks Zig master.
caveats: Port of an already-listed project (simdjson), so it may fold into it as a duplicate. The 2 ms wall time of a whole process is dominated by process start-up, dynamic loading of libstdc++ and file reading rather than parsing 630 KB of JSON, and the instruction count is slightly higher for Zig (+1.7%), so the 12.9% gap and the RSS gap most likely reflect start-up and linking differences rather than parser speed (my inference). CPU model not stated, single file, single run of the harness; the README's older plot compares against Go, Nim and Zig std only as an image.
found_via: WebSearch: 'Zig library benchmark vs simdjson OR libdeflate OR zstd ...' (github.com results) surfaced travisstaloch/simdjzon; opened README and commits page.

name: hexdump-rs (Rust hexdump -C replacement)
baseline: system hexdump -C (C; implementation and version not stated, likely util-linux or BSD hexdump)
workload: Canonical hex+ASCII dump (hexdump -C) of four files with hyperfine -m 100 --warmup 5: 10 MB from /dev/random, a 7.8 MB semi-random file (test.mca), an 8.5 MB file whose lines all differ (no squeezing) and a 1.1 GB file of zeros.
claimed_speedup: Hyperfine screenshots in the README (img/*.png): dev-random 708.6 ms vs 16.9 ms (42.00x faster); test.mca 617.1 ms vs 16.0 ms (38.62x); no-squeeze.bin 646.3 ms vs 17.1 ms (37.86x); zeros.bin 658.2 ms vs 338.5 ms (1.94x). README text says 'up to a 14x speedup' while the repository description says 'up to 40x faster'.
compiler_and_flags: cargo release build (./target/release/hexdump-rs); Cargo.toml release profile only adds debug = true for flamegraphs; no C build flags (system hexdump binary as installed).
tradeoffs: Implements only hexdump -C, not hexdump's format-string language, and is 'meant as a drop-in replacement for hexdump -C' only.
caveats: Different algorithm: the system hexdump drives a generic format-string interpreter while this tool hard-codes the one canonical layout, so the 40x gap is a specialisation effect, not a language effect (my inference; the README gives no mechanism). CPU, OS, hexdump version and output destination are not stated, the numbers exist only as images, and the README text (14x) disagrees with the screenshots (up to 42x). The zeros.bin row (1.94x) is where both tools squeeze repeated lines. Tiny hobby repo with no stars.
found_via: WebSearch: 'Rust rewrite of C tool faster than original C benchmark hyperfine github faster than GNU' surfaced the hexdump-rs README; opened the README, the four screenshots and the commits page.

name: Koka (Perceus reference counting): deriv benchmark vs C++ gcc 9.3.0
baseline: C++ (gcc 9.3.0) version of the symbolic-derivative benchmark in test/bench/cpp; it never reclaims memory, per the README
workload: deriv: symbolic derivative of a large expression, an allocation-heavy benchmark with little computation.
claimed_speedup: README chart (values printed on the bars, relative to Koka = 1.00): execution time C++ 1.33 (Koka 1.33x faster); peak working set C++ 2.25x of Koka. Same chart, other rows: cfold C++ 3.33x slower than Koka; rbtree C++ 0.92 and nqueens C++ 0.79 (C++ faster than Koka there).
compiler_and_flags: Koka 2.0.3 compiled to C and built with gcc 9.3.0 (flags not stated in the README; test/bench builds through CMake, default build type Release); C++ built with gcc 9.3.0.
hardware: 3.8 GHz AMD 3600XT, Ubuntu 20.04, November 2020; averages over 10 runs
tradeoffs: Reference counting with in-place reuse needs no tracing GC but adds refcount work and cannot reclaim cycles; Koka compiles through C so any C toolchain can build it; much smaller ecosystem than C++.
caveats: Numbers are read from a chart image in the README and come from Koka 2.0.3 in November 2020 (Koka is now at v3.2.x); flags are not in the README. The README says the C++ baseline is not like-for-like: 'we either use in-place updates without supporting persistence (as in rbtree which uses std::map) or we do not reclaim memory at all (as in deriv, nqueens, and cfold)'. The same chart shows C++ ahead on rbtree (0.92) and nqueens (0.79), and the Java bar is faster than Koka on deriv (0.86). The Perceus PLDI 2021 paper has the same benchmarks but was not opened (blocked), so this stays first-party tier C.
found_via: GitHub: README of koka-lang/koka (benchmark section and chart doc/bench-amd3600-nov-2020.png), listed as a lead without numbers by the sys papers search; I read the values printed on the chart bars.
why_faster: Source (README): precise Perceus reference counting with reuse analysis, compiled to C 'without needing a garbage collector or runtime system'; the README frames the benchmarks as showing reference counting is viable and competitive, not as a direct absolute-speed comparison across languages.

name: Nim 2.2.10 (ref objects): benchLANG binary trees vs C and C++ at -O3
baseline: C (GCC 16.2.0: gcc -O3 -march=native -flto -funroll-loops -ffp-contract=off) and C++ (g++ -std=c++20, same flags); both malloc/new every node and free (delete) it inside the timed region
workload: CLBG-style binary trees, depths 4 to 18: allocate, check and drop complete binary trees of individually allocated nodes; benchLANG's fifth workload (the others are primes, Fibonacci(45), strings and Mandelbrot).
claimed_speedup: README results table (September 2026, one run per language): Nim 0.809 s vs C 1.010 s and C++ 1.147 s on binary trees, about 1.25x faster than C and 1.42x faster than C++ (derived from page data). Other columns, Nim vs C: primes 2.725 vs 2.725 s, Fibonacci 1.716 vs 1.694 s, strings 2.804 vs 2.132 s, Mandelbrot 2.244 vs 2.201 s; total 10.298 s vs 9.762 s, so C is faster overall.
compiler_and_flags: Nim 2.2.10: nim c --nimcache:nimcache -d:danger -d:lto --panics:on --passC:-march=native --passC:-ffp-contract=off --passL:-s (C backend compiler not stated, nixpkgs GCC 16.2.0 presumably); C: gcc -O3 -march=native -flto -funroll-loops -ffp-contract=off -s; C++: g++ -std=c++20 with the same flags. Toolchains pinned with Nix.
hardware: AMD Ryzen 9 5900X locked at 3.5 GHz, 48 GB DDR4-3600 CL16, Arch Linux; one run per language, 3 September 2026
tradeoffs: Peak RSS for the whole process is 51.5 MiB for Nim vs 33.3 MiB for C; Nim loses to C on the strings workload (2.804 s vs 2.132 s).
caveats: The source gives no mechanism, which caps this at tier C. Reading languages/Nim/bench.nim and languages/C/bench.c (my inference): Nim uses 'ref object' nodes with no explicit free, so the runtime's own allocator and deterministic reference counting do the allocation and freeing, while C pays glibc malloc and free per node; a pooled or arena C version would likely erase the gap. One run per language, one machine, tiny suite, the README says its inputs are compile-time constants. Other languages beat C on this workload too (Java 0.347 s, OCaml 0.865 s, C# 0.931 s, Bun 0.816 s, Fortran 0.986 s), which points at allocator behaviour rather than Nim.
found_via: GitHub: raw README of GlebOlsen/benchLANG (the repo surfaced in the WebSearch 'faster than the C implementation benchmark Rust OR Zig OR Nim OR D'); I read every language column and the Nim and C sources. Sibling searches recorded Java, OCaml, C# and Zig rows from the same table; Nim was not recorded.

name: V (gcc backend) in kostya/benchmarks: Brainfuck bench.b
baseline: C++ (g++ 16.1.0, -std=c++23 -O3 -march=native -flto=auto) 1.097 s; also C/gcc 1.112 s, C/clang 1.136 s and C++/clang++ 1.167 s
workload: Brainfuck interpreter running bench.b, the suite's first brainfuck sample; the same interpreter design (op tree, tape vector) ported to each language.
claimed_speedup: README bench.b table (median s): V/gcc 0.985 vs C++/g++ 1.097 (about 1.11x faster), C/gcc 1.112 (1.13x), C/clang 1.136, C++/clang++ 1.167 (derived from page data). Rust 1.008 and D/ldc2 1.078 are also ahead of C++/g++, while Zig 1.327, Nim/gcc 1.171 and V/clang 1.846 are slower. On mandel.b the C++/g++ row (10.143 s) beats V/gcc (17.865 s).
compiler_and_flags: common/commands.mk: V: v -prod -no-bounds-checking -prealloc -cc gcc with -cflags '-O3 -march=native -flto=auto ...'; C++: g++ -O3 -march=native -flto=auto -std=c++23; C: gcc -O3 -march=native -flto=auto -std=c23. V 0.5.2 (7647ce1), gcc and g++ 16.1.0, clang 22.1.8.
hardware: Intel Xeon E-2324G, Debian forky/sid Docker image, README updated 2026-07-19
tradeoffs: V emits C that gcc compiles, so this reflects V's generated code through the gcc backend; with -no-bounds-checking and -prealloc the safety defaults are off.
caveats: Capped at tier C because the source states no mechanism. Only the gcc backend wins: V/clang is 1.846 s, slower than every C and C++ row, and on mandel.b V is slower than C++. The margin over C++/g++ (about 10%) is the kind of difference that implementation details (Op struct layout, vector growth) can produce; the V, C++ and C versions are community-written ports of one design, not byte-identical programs. Single machine, median of repeated runs (±0.001 s).
found_via: GitHub: raw README and common/commands.mk of kostya/benchmarks (sibling searches recorded the Rust bench.b row; V was not recorded); I compared every C, C++, Rust, Zig, D, Nim, V, Odin and C3 row of all five tests against the best C or C++ row.

name: Zig compiler (zig build-exe) compile throughput vs gcc and g++ in nordlow/compiler-benchmark
baseline: C (gcc 15.3.0 and 16.2.1, clang 23.1.1) and C++ (g++ 15.3.0 and 16.2.1, clang++ 23.1.1) compiling the same generated arithmetic translation unit
workload: nordlow/compiler-benchmark: compile (and run) one massive synthetic translation unit of arithmetic call chains, reported as microseconds per generated function ('Total=Build+Run [us/f]'), untemplated and templated variants.
claimed_speedup: README table, Total=Build+Run us/f (untemplated / templated): Zig 110 / 92 vs C gcc-15 392, C gcc-16 454, C++ g++-15 303 / 600, C++ g++-16 486 / 566, C clang 118, C++ clang++ 236 / 107. About 3.6x faster than gcc-15 and 4.1x faster than gcc-16 on C (derived from page data) and on par with clang C (118 vs 110, 7%). Slower than tcc 4, dmd 13, cuik 76 and cproc 86 in the same suite.
compiler_and_flags: Compiler versions are listed in the README table (zig 0.18.0-dev.35, odin dev-2026-09, c3c 0.8.5, rustc 1.100.0-nightly, gcc 15.3.0 and 16.2.1, clang 23.1.1); the README calls the test 'unoptimized code-generation scaling' and does not document optimization flags for any compiler.
hardware: AMD Ryzen AI 7 350 (8+8 cores) at 5.09 GHz, Arch Linux, sample run as of 2026-09
tradeoffs: Compile speed only; the generated executables are about 12x larger per function than gcc's (1,503 vs 121 B/f).
caveats: Compile-time comparison on one synthetic file of arithmetic call chains with no headers, standard library or module resolution (the README says it does not reflect real builds), not the usual run-time -O3 comparison; C and C++ flags are undocumented so optimization levels are unmatched. The GitHub repository of Zig says 'Moved to Codeberg' and its last GitHub commit is 2025-11-27, so metadata here is a pointer, not the live repository. Zig's output is 1,422 to 1,503 B per function against 121 B for gcc (README: runtime scaffolding and unwinding metadata). The sibling record for D (dmd) is from the same table. Independent suite, but a small one (167 stars) and one machine.
found_via: GitHub: README of nordlow/compiler-benchmark (found by the sys shootouts search for D; this row and the other systems-language rows of the same table were not recorded there).
why_faster: README: Zig shows near-zero generic overhead (97 vs 92 us/f untemplated vs templated) thanks to comptime evaluation of uniform scalar types; the README groups Zig with odin as 'neck-and-neck with clang' and does not name a mechanism for the gap to gcc beyond the heavy GCC front end and backend.

workload: nordlow/compiler-benchmark: compile (and run) one massive synthetic translation unit of arithmetic call chains, reported as microseconds per generated function ('Total=Build+Run [us/f]'), untemplated and templated variants.
claimed_speedup: README table, Total=Build+Run us/f (untemplated / templated): rustc 187 / 238 vs C gcc-15 392, C gcc-16 454, C++ g++-15 303 / 600, C++ g++-16 486 / 566. About 2.1x faster than gcc-15 and 2.4x faster than gcc-16 on C untemplated, and 2.5x faster than g++-15 templated (derived from page data). The README highlights 'rustc (187 µs/f) significantly outpaces GCC-based C/C++ (~450–486 µs/f)'.
compiler_and_flags: Compiler versions are listed in the README table (zig 0.18.0-dev.35, odin dev-2026-09, c3c 0.8.5, rustc 1.100.0-nightly, gcc 15.3.0 and 16.2.1, clang 23.1.1); the README calls the test 'unoptimized code-generation scaling' and does not document optimization flags for any compiler.
hardware: AMD Ryzen AI 7 350 (8+8 cores) at 5.09 GHz, Arch Linux, sample run as of 2026-09
tradeoffs: Compile speed only; rustc adds +30% build time for templated (generic) code in this suite.
caveats: Compile-time comparison on one synthetic file of arithmetic call chains with no headers, standard library or module resolution (the README says it does not reflect real builds), not the usual run-time -O3 comparison; C and C++ flags are undocumented so optimization levels are unmatched. rustc is slower than clang C (118 us/f), clang++ templated (107 us/f), Zig, Odin and C3 in the same table, and the Rust row includes full borrow checking and type checking while GCC and clang skip some C++ semantic checks (README note). The check time alone is 86 us/f untemplated. The sibling record for D (dmd) is from the same table. Independent suite, but a small one (167 stars) and one machine.
found_via: GitHub: README of nordlow/compiler-benchmark (found by the sys shootouts search for D; this row and the other systems-language rows of the same table were not recorded there).
why_faster: README: the README says rustc 'handily outperforms' the GCC front ends and notes that GCC and clang skip some C++ semantic checks that Rustc performs in full; no further mechanism is given.
